title: Perfect secrecy & breaking codes
covers: One-time pad, entropy, frequency analysis, cryptanalysis
learningGoals: You will be able to explain why the One-Time Pad achieves mathematically perfect secrecy.
You will be able to perform frequency analysis to crack simple ciphers.
You will be able to differentiate ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, and chosen-plaintext attacks.

lessonCards.title: The One-Time Pad (OTP)
lessonCards.analogy: A secret key as long as the book itself, used once on a single page, then burned in fire.
lessonCards.coreConcept: A truly random key of equal length to the plaintext, used exactly once, provides unbreakable perfect secrecy (proven by Claude Shannon).
lessonCards.example: A 5-letter word XORed with 5 truly random bytes produces ciphertext that could equally decrypt to any 5-letter word.

lessonCards.title: Why Reusing OTP is Catastrophic
lessonCards.analogy: Writing two letters on the same carbon copy paper leaves visible overlapping pencil grooves.
lessonCards.coreConcept: If key K is reused: C1 XOR C2 = (P1 XOR K) XOR (P2 XOR K) = P1 XOR P2. The secret key cancels out entirely!
lessonCards.example: Soviet code clerks reused OTP pages in the 1940s, allowing the Venona project to decrypt sensitive diplomatic cables.

lessonCards.title: Cryptanalysis Attack Models
lessonCards.analogy: A detective with only a locked letter vs a detective who also found the sender's rough draft.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Ciphertext-only is the hardest attack. Known-plaintext pairs sample input and output. Chosen-plaintext lets the attacker inject custom plaintexts.
lessonCards.example: Chosen-plaintext is standard for evaluating modern ciphers: if you can choose the input, can you recover the key?

questions.prompt: According to Claude Shannon, why is a properly implemented One-Time Pad mathematically UNBREAKABLE?
options: Every possible plaintext of that length is equally probable to an eavesdropper
The key is encrypted by RSA first
Computers crash when calculating XOR
The ciphertext is always 0
questions.explanation: Given ciphertext C, brute-forcing all possible keys produces every valid English sentence of that length with zero information about which was real.
wrongExplanations: Correct! With a truly random key used once, ciphertext gives zero information about plaintext.
OTP requires no public-key encryption.
XOR is the fastest CPU instruction available.
Ciphertext consists of uniformly distributed random bytes.
questions.realWorldExample: The Washington-Moscow hotline used One-Time Pad teleprinters during the Cold War.

questions.prompt: What fatal flaw happens if an operator reuses the same One-Time Pad key K on two different messages P1 and P2?
options: XORing the two ciphertexts together cancels the key: C1 XOR C2 = P1 XOR P2
The computer processor overheats
The messages turn into blank whitespace
The encryption speed drops by 50%
questions.explanation: C1 XOR C2 = (P1 XOR K) XOR (P2 XOR K) = P1 XOR P2. The key disappears, allowing frequency analysis of P1 and P2.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Reusing a one-time pad leaks the XOR of the plaintexts directly.
Processing XOR has no abnormal thermal impact on hardware.
Data remains binary values.
XOR throughput is unchanged.
questions.realWorldExample: The US Venona project decrypted thousands of Soviet spy cables because codebooks were duplicated.

questions.prompt: In cryptanalysis, what is a 'Chosen-Plaintext Attack' (CPA)?
options: The attacker chooses arbitrary plaintext messages and obtains matching ciphertexts
The attacker has only intercept access to ciphertext bytes
The attacker already knows the secret master key
The attacker bribes the system administrator
questions.explanation: In a chosen-plaintext attack, the cryptanalyst feeds crafted inputs into the black-box cipher to observe how outputs change.
wrongExplanations: Correct! CPA allows defenders to test whether differential patterns leak secret key bits.
Having only ciphertext is a Ciphertext-Only Attack.
If the key is already known, no cryptanalysis attack is needed.
Bribing administrators is social engineering.
questions.realWorldExample: Modern block cipher standards like AES must be mathematically proven secure against Chosen-Plaintext Attacks.

questions.prompt: What is the most frequent single letter in standard English prose used in frequency analysis?
options: E (approx. 12.7%)
Z (approx. 15%)
X (approx. 20%)
Q (approx. 18%)
questions.explanation: Letter 'E' occurs most frequently in English text (approx. 12.7%), followed by 'T', 'A', and 'O'.
wrongExplanations: Correct! 'E' is the highest frequency letter in standard English.
'Z' is one of the rarest letters (< 0.1%).
'X' is extremely rare (< 0.2%).
'Q' is also extremely rare (< 0.1%).
questions.realWorldExample: Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes story 'The Dancing Men' used letter 'E' frequency to crack the code.

questions.prompt: What practical obstacle prevents the One-Time Pad from being used for all internet web traffic?
options: Key distribution: securely sharing keys as long as every message is impractical
XOR arithmetic is too slow for mobile phones
Fiber-optic cables cannot carry pad bits
Browsers do not support addition
questions.explanation: If you already have a secure channel to transmit gigabytes of random OTP keys, you could just send the message itself on that channel!
wrongExplanations: Correct! Securely distributing huge quantities of pre-shared keys at global scale is logistically impossible.
XOR is the fastest mathematical operation possible.
Fiber optics carry arbitrary binary data.
Browsers execute complete cryptographic suites.
questions.realWorldExample: Modern SSL/TLS solves key distribution by using asymmetric cryptography instead of bulk pre-shared pads.

questions.prompt: What is 'Kerckhoffs's Principle', the foundation of modern cryptography?
options: A cryptosystem must be secure even if everything about it is public, except the key
Security algorithms must always be kept secret commercial property
Keys should never exceed 8 bits
Only government military officials may read cipher code
questions.explanation: Auguste Kerckhoffs stated in 1883 that security through obscurity fails; security must depend solely on key secrecy.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Public algorithms peer-reviewed by global mathematicians prove security without hidden secrets.
Security through obscurity is widely condemned.
8-bit keys can be cracked in less than a microsecond.
Open public standards protect civil liberties and online banking.
questions.realWorldExample: AES and RSA are completely open public standards; knowing their code provides zero help in guessing the key.

ashRecap: The One-Time Pad is the only truly unbreakable cipher, but only if the key is completely random, as long as the message, and never reused!
